When i moved to Linux i used to work on Windows 2000. It was a good OS, several orders of magnitude better than Windows 95/98/ME. I've always been a DOS/Windows programmer and, back then, i used to use Delphi as my main programming environment and i really enjoyed it. Unfortunately one day i found out that my hard disk was corrupted, the partition was broken and the computer refused to boot, after some horrible moments i managed to make it boot again and thankfully my source code was intact (here i learned about the importance of backups), but at that point i didn't want to trust Windows with my data anymore (much later i found out that it wasn't Windows corrupting my data, but a memory [RAM] module that went subtly bad... it didn't give any evident error or crash, it just randomly corrupted data). I was angry at Windows and Microsoft and feared that this would happen again, besides i didn't like the new version that came out a few months before... XP looked like a toy in my eyes, an attempt to make computers just as dumb as TVs, so that is why i went from Windows to Linux.

Back then i didn't know anything about Linux, but i figured i would learn, i really didn't want to lose my precious data, and in few months i had mastered Linux well enough to know how it worked quite deeply. I loved the Terminal with its thousands commands and the fact that the GUI was only "just another program" and could be skipped entirely (i never really liked GUIs, i loved DOS back when i was a teen and i loved the Turbo Vision TUI https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/it/4/4d/TurboVision.jpg that i learned to master in my softwares back at the time of Turbo Pascal for DOS). I also loved the fact that most, if not all, of the programs, including the OS itself, was opensource, which meant that if i really cared enough i could learn its deepest "secrets".

To help me transition Borland had developed a version of Delphi that would run and compile softwares for Linux, it was called Kylix and it was great https://edn.embarcadero.com/article/images/22417/snapshot01.gif , it used OO-Pascal just like Delphi and had a CLX that was very similar to Delphi's VCL, just like Delphi on Windows you could literally draw your user interface (a thing that was pretty much unheard of in Linux back then) so all you had to do was write your code and let Kylix do the rest. It was not as good as Delphi on Windows, but close enough (actually very close) to make you productive in very little time... if you knew Delphi you were pretty much already a good Kylix programmer. It came with many-many common use visual components and some components that were missing i developed them myself and released as opensource to the Kylix community (some were also featured on Borland's website).

But as i found out it wasn't going to last... Microsoft back then was pretty anti-Linux and they did everything in their power to sabotage it. They saw that Kylix was a HUGE step forward into porting professional software to Linux and a HUGE threat to Windows, Kylix was the best RAD [Rapid Application Development tool] out there for Linux (the only one perhaps), so they feared that more and more developers would "jump ship" and move their software to Linux and their users with them.

Not only was Kylix the best RAD, but the programs it made were "self-sufficient", in short they were really easy to install because they required very little dependencies on the Linux side, it pretty much made executables that would just run out of the box no matter which linux distro you were using. So, if my memory assists me well, they bought a piece of Borland (the company who was making Delphi and Linux).

In few years Delphi abandoned Win32 to move to .NET (which, IMO was a dumb choice back then, on .NET you already had tools such as Visual Studio that supported more languages [mainly VB.NET and C#] and was cheaper than Delphi) and, as odd as it might seem, abandoned Kylix entirely, just like that, without even an announcement. So that was the end of Kylix on Linux and with it its hope to see professional grade software easily ported on Linux.

I tried to protest on Borland's and Delphi's newsgroups (back then newsgroups were still a thing, web-forums were still too small and young), but, again as odd as it might seem, they (the newsgroups) were literally invaded by odd and never seen before guys telling us that everything was fine, that Borland would have never abandoned Kylix and that Linux was still going to be supported. I didn't believe a word, i kept protesting, but they made it look to the other developers like people protesting were just a bunch of lunatics. Guess this lunatic was right though, since the development of Kylix stopped there and Delphi, from one of the main players in the Windows development field, became pretty much unknown in a matter of years.

Anyways, now i was on a OS that i mostly liked, but where my knowledge and skills were mostly useless. I didn't really like any of the development tools on Linux, compared to what i had before it was like going back in time 20 years or more (at least if you wanted something professionally looking and didn't want to spend ages typing several of lines of code just to have a freaking visual component on a simple form, a thing that on Delphi/Kylix you used to do with a simple drag&drop) and, what's worse, installing software that wasn't already pre-compiled and included in the repos of my distro was hard and time consuming even for a developer like me (i never liked C/C++ so it was always very challenging for me even to just understand why the damn thing refused to compile) especially if your distro didn't come with the right version of the libraries the software needed to compile.

For my job i had another computer where i used Windows and Visual Studio (i decided to abandon Delphi the moment it jumped on the .NET ship, there was simply no reason to keep using Delphi at that point), i begun to like again Windows and the Microsoft tools (after all i spent most of my life on Microsoft development tools, beginning with BASIC when i was a kid) and i found myself spending more and more time on Windows than Linux until the Linux computer was pretty much abandoned.

So that's the short and simplified version of how i went from Windows to Linux and then back again.
